newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin seeks loyal support from French Socialists.
newsitem.headline: Jospin seeks loyal support from French Socialists.

text.p: Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, facing criticism from political allies after barely a month in power, asked members of his Socialist Party on Saturday to "respect the rules of the game" and loyally support his agenda.
In a speech to party leaders in Paris, Jospin pledged to listen to their advice on national policy and, in return, they could share in the leftist government's successes.
"Our success will be collective," Jospin told the closed-door meeting, according to spokesman Manuel Valls.
"Nothing will be done without your advice. The Socialists will be closely involved in all decisions," Valls quoted him as saying. "There will be no grumpy spectators."
The leftist government combining Socialists, Communists and Greens took power from the previous rightist majority after an upset victory in a June 1 parliamentary election.
Just one month later, it faces criticism from its own ranks as well as trade unions, family associations and opposition politicians over some of its early moves.

Family groups criticise Jospin's plan to focus family subsidies on the poorest families. Unions question his slow pace in implementing campaign promises to create 700,000 new jobs and trim the working week to 35 hours from 39 without a cut in pay.
Opposition politicians wonder whether he will honour French commitments to bring France into European economic and monetary union by meeting requirements for the euro.
"It is not fair to expect us to achieve in 30 days what the others could not achieve in four years," Socialist Party number two Francois Hollande grumbled to reporters.
An IPSOS opinion poll for France 2 television released on Saturday suggested that the French people agreed with Hollande.

It found that 76 percent felt that Jospin should take his time in setting out his economic programme while just 21 percent said he should move quickly. The poll of 1,102 people was conducted on Friday and Saturday.
But what appeared to hurt the most was criticism from Communist and Socialist allies in parliament of his handling of the closing of a Renault car assembly plant in Belgium.
Jospin has insisted he kept a campaign promise to review Renault's decision though the plant will still close.
Thanks to his review, some plant workers will be redeployed and there will be no outright layoffs, he boasted earlier this week. The French state owns 46 percent of Renault's shares.
Jospin told the congress of party officials from across France, convened to prepare for a larger congress in the western city of Brest in November, that internal criticism was particularly damaging.
"If the first criticisms, the first incitements to disenchantment, come from our own ranks, how will we convince the others?" he asked.

He said the state's weakened finances and social woes would oblige his government to make hard choices but said his top priorities remained to create jobs, battle social inequity, boost economic growth and honour France's European commitments.
Representatives of the Socialists' left-most wing said at the close of the day they were not fully satisfied with the prime minister's performance.
"There is disagreement over methods," said senator Jean-Luc Melenchon. announcing his faction would propose an alternative programme at the Brest congress.
